extracted.intended_audience: performers/companies (comedy/theatre/physical theatre) planning to take a show to the Edinburgh Fringe
extracted.subtask_short: taking a show to edinburgh fringe
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, timeline-based guidance for performers or groups planning a run at the Edinburgh Fringe, covering choice of Free vs Paid model, venue applications, promotion, press, and on-the-ground logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research the official edfringe.com site early
rubrics_metrics.description: Research www.edfringe.com. September and October. Go to the participants section and read guides like How to Sell a Show, Venues etc to get a good understanding of how the Fringe works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read through all relevant participant guides early (Sept/Oct) so you understand processes, deadlines and expectations; this is 'the best' site and run by the Fringe organisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide between Free Fringe and Paid Fringe
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide if you’re going Free Fringe or Paid Fringe. October/November.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make this decision early (Oct/Nov) because it affects application paths, costs and promotion strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free Fringe: advantages and disadvantages
rubrics_metrics.description: On the Free Fringe you don’t sell tickets, you perform for free, and then have a donations bucket at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages listed: less initial costs (no guarantees), easier to get a large audience if new, increasingly respected, possible luck with great venues, can still make decent money, easier to get in. Disadvantages: some venues may be poor, limited profit potential (though exceptions exist), hard to do theatrical shows, audience changes the style of show possible, less likely to attract major publicity. Note two main Free Fringe organisations (PBH’s Free Fringe and Laughing Horse) — you can apply to one but not the other; read their sites thoroughly and be aware you’ll be promoting all Free Fringe shows, not just yours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid Fringe: advantages and disadvantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Paid Fringe means charging the public and ticket sales go through box office/online; you must apply to venues and often pay a guarantee/deposit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: nicer venues, professional support, higher profile, easier to get press, able to do more theatrical shows, possibility of making profit. Disadvantages: large financial investment/guarantees (around £3,000 at least), larger financial risk, harder to get large audiences for a new group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply to venues before registering with the Fringe
rubrics_metrics.description: You apply to venues first to get a venue to perform in. They are selective. Once you have that sorted you sign up to the Fringe in general through www.edfringe.com.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fringe registration itself is not selective — securing a venue is the gate. Prioritise venue applications and only register programme entry after venue confirmation; keep track of each venue's requirements and timescales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and shortlist suitable venues
rubrics_metrics.description: Go through the list of all venues on edfringe.com and make a shortlist of suitable places based on space, similar programming and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for venues with the right space that do similar stuff and have a good reputation; proximity (e.g., to Royal Mile) can help. Each venue has its own application timescales and requirements — be on top of these early. Examples of venues and rough profiles are provided (Pleasance Courtyard, Assembly Rooms, Pleasance Dome, C Venues, Zoo, Underbelly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply to multiple venues to increase chances
rubrics_metrics.description: You can actually apply to all venues to increase your chances of getting in somewhere; have a perfect venue in mind but also backups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying widely worked for the author; exception is PBH Free Fringe who prefer you apply only to them if choosing that route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage initial contact and ongoing communications with venues
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial batch of applications followed by ongoing communication; timescales vary between venues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every communication matters — good graphics and materials can influence venue placement (e.g., getting bumped to a nicer space). Keep relationships professional and responsive through Nov–Jan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for offers, confirmations and possible deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: Offers from venues typically come Feb/March. If you're paid fringe you might have to pay a hefty deposit around this time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track deadlines and financial commitments carefully; timescales vary and some venues leave decisions late, impacting programme submission timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programme entry must attract and convert audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: The programme entry should attract attention, explain what the show actually is, why people should go and see it, and raise desire in the audience to see your show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People do go and watch shows based on the programme entry. Write from the point of view of benefits to the audience (why should they see it?), include reviews/quotes to 'seal the deal', use a good image, and avoid sounding off-putting ('don’t sound like a dick'). Make sure you meet programme deadlines (March/April).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and print flyers and posters to professional standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Flyers and posters are extremely important; invest in good graphic design and reliable printing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can’t do graphic design, hire someone. A bad flyer will put people off; a good flyer should have an eye-catching image that captures the mood and sells the show, be not too wordy, include short reviews/star ratings and the show title. On the back include core details (where, when, how much, dates) laid out clearly, plus a blurb written from the audience-benefit perspective. Posters should match flyer branding. Use reliable printers even if more expensive to avoid last-minute disasters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use flyering as the key method of persuading people to attend
rubrics_metrics.description: You persuade people to come to see your show through flyering; the author reports direct correlation between flyering hours and audience numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate substantial time to flyering (e.g., 4 hours a day led to full houses), and ensure flyers are high quality — poor flyers waste flyering effort and can actively deter potential audience members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep advertising on-brand and pursue affordable channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising depends on your budget; online and apps can work and there are opportunities in the Fringe programme advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research deals, spot low-cost opportunities, and ensure adverts/flyers/posters/programme entry deliver the same key message and visual brand to maximise recognition and recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start press outreach early and get listed
rubrics_metrics.description: The edfringe.com media team can provide a press contact sheet. Get press releases and listings out before the programme comes out in June so press are aware of you when choosing what to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some press are more useful than others; getting listed widely increases chances of discovery. Begin press work in May/June/July and maintain professional, timely contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan accommodation and budget for it (expect it to be the biggest expense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accommodation is the biggest expense. People commonly share rooms to reduce costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor accommodation into your budget early and plan shared housing with others to lower per-person cost; no detailed tips provided beyond acknowledging its costliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider other fringes for one-off or smaller shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Other fringes (e.g., Brighton, Buxton) may be good for one-off shows or smaller runs and are worth considering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brighton is good for one-off shows; Buxton is increasingly popular — consider these as alternatives or stepping stones rather than full Edinburgh-style runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Super basics checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Core simple truths: you have a show in a venue (free or paid), you raise awareness through advertising/posters/press, you persuade people via flyering, you live in shared housing, and you apply to venues then sign up to Fringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a high-level mental checklist of the essential elements to organise when planning an Edinburgh run.
